metadata.title: Textual Rhetoric Database
metadata.description: Comprehensive reference database for textual rhetorical analysis and construction

schema.overview: This part of rhetoric explains the systematic five-stage workflow used to transform an initial concept into a fully realized and delivered piece of communication.
schema.core_question: Through which specific phases of production must I progress to ensure my message is thoroughly researched, organized, and presented?

inventio.name: Invention/Discovery
inventio.definition: The discovery and brainstorming phase where you identify the strongest arguments and evidence available for your subject.
key_characteristics: Analysis of available data and sources
examples: A journalist researching multiple sources before writing an investigative article
A lawyer gathering case law and precedents before crafting an argument
A scientist reviewing literature before proposing a hypothesis

dispositio.name: Arrangement
dispositio.definition: The strategic arrangement of those arguments into a coherent structure (such as introduction, body, and conclusion) to maximize impact.
examples: An essay structured with introduction, three body paragraphs, and conclusion
A speech arranged to build from weakest to strongest argument
A report organized by problem-solution structure

elocutio.name: Style
elocutio.definition: The stylistic 'texture' of the text, focusing on precise word choice and the application of rhetorical figures to suit the audience.
examples: Academic writing using formal, precise language
Marketing copy using vivid, emotive language
Technical documentation using clear, unambiguous terminology

memoria.name: Memory
memoria.definition: The use of mnemonic systems and cognitive techniques to internalize the content for a fluid, natural delivery.
examples: A speaker using the method of loci to remember speech points
Repeated motifs in a novel that create thematic coherence
Acronyms or mnemonic devices embedded in educational content

pronuntiatio.name: Delivery/Performance
pronuntiatio.definition: The final execution of the message, focusing on physical appearance, vocal modulation, and the use of gesture to command the room.
examples: A TED talk delivered with confident body language and vocal variation
A poem performed with attention to rhythm and pause
A business presentation using professional slides and clear speaking

proofs.overview: These represent the primary modes of persuasion used to establish validity and influence the perspective or behavior of an audience.
proofs.core_question: What specific types of evidence and appeals must I employ to establish my authority and convince the audience that my claims are true?

ethos.name: Credibility/Character
ethos.definition: Establishing credibility and trust by demonstrating the speaker's reliable character, expertise, and moral standing.
examples: A doctor citing medical research and professional experience
A witness testimony in court demonstrating personal reliability
An author establishing credentials in a preface or bio

pathos.name: Emotion
pathos.definition: Generating credibility and engagement by appealing to the audience's emotions, creating a visceral or empathetic connection to the topic.
examples: Charity advertisements showing suffering to motivate donations
A memorial speech evoking grief and remembrance
Political rhetoric appealing to hope, fear, or anger

logos.name: Logic/Reason
logos.definition: Building credibility through logical reasoning, the presentation of data, and the use of structured evidence to support a rational conclusion.
examples: A scientific paper presenting data analysis and conclusions
A legal brief using precedents and logical reasoning
A financial report showing statistical trends and projections

tropes.overview: This part of rhetoric focuses on the imaginative impact of the text, using non-literal ways to shift meaning and engage the audience's imagination.
tropes.core_question: How can I transform standard language into imaginative figures to make a concept feel richer, more evocative, and conceptually deep?

resemblance.name: Metaphor/Simile
resemblance.definition: Figures like metaphor and simile that create meaning by comparing two distinct things based on shared traits.
key_characteristics: Transfers qualities from one domain to another
examples: Time is money (metaphor)
Her smile was as bright as the sun (simile)
The world is a stage (metaphor)

association.name: Metonymy
association.definition: Figures like metonymy that substitute a word for something closely related to it.
examples: The White House announced... (building for administration)
The pen is mightier than the sword (tools for writing/warfare)
Silicon Valley leads innovation (place for tech industry)

naming.name: Synecdoche
naming.definition: Substituting labels to identify subjects indirectly, such as synecdoche, where a part represents the whole.
key_characteristics: Part represents whole or vice versa
Specific for general or vice versa
examples: All hands on deck (hands for sailors)
Nice wheels! (wheels for car)
The law (the law for police/legal system)

invention.name: Neologism/Creative Language
invention.definition: The creative stretching of language to describe the 'indescribable' or using parts of speech in new ways (e.g., turning a noun into a verb).
examples: Let's Google that (noun to verb)
The bling of the jewelry (onomatopoeia/new word)
Unfriend (creative combination)

extendedmeaning.name: Allegory/Irony
extendedmeaning.definition: Large-scale figures like allegory or irony where the surface meaning masks a deeper, sustained secondary interpretation.
examples: George Orwell's Animal Farm (political allegory)
Saying 'What lovely weather' during a storm (irony)
Biblical parables (allegorical teaching)

ornamentalepithet.name: Descriptive Tags
ornamentalepithet.definition: The use of descriptive, often formulaic, adjectives or tags to characterize a person or object with vivid intensity.
examples: Swift-footed Achilles (Homeric epithet)
The Great Emancipator (for Lincoln)
The rosy-fingered dawn (Homer)

fallacies.overview: This part of rhetoric focuses on the rational impact of the text.

fallacy.name: Logical Errors
fallacy.definition: Identifying and labeling common errors in reasoning.

common_types.name: Ad Hominem
common_types.description: Attacking the person rather than the argument
common_types.example: You can't trust his climate research because he owns an SUV

common_types.name: Straw Man
common_types.description: Misrepresenting an argument to make it easier to attack
common_types.example: Environmentalists want us all to live in caves

common_types.name: False Dichotomy
common_types.description: Presenting only two options when more exist
common_types.example: You're either with us or against us

common_types.name: Slippery Slope
common_types.description: Arguing that one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences
common_types.example: If we allow same-sex marriage, people will want to marry animals

common_types.name: Appeal to Authority
common_types.example: This must be true because a celebrity said it

common_types.name: Hasty Generalization
common_types.example: I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there must be rude

common_types.name: Post Hoc
common_types.example: I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks caused the victory

common_types.name: Circular Reasoning
common_types.description: Using the conclusion as a premise
common_types.example: The Bible is true because it says so in the Bible

common_types.name: Red Herring
common_types.example: Why worry about climate change when there are starving children?

common_types.name: Appeal to Emotion
common_types.description: Manipulating emotions instead of using logic
common_types.example: Think of the children! (without relevant connection)

fallacy_flipside.name: Legitimate Uses
fallacy_flipside.definition: Recognizing the legitimate versions of these rational mistakes.
key_characteristics: Valid forms of seemingly fallacious reasoning
Strategic use of emotion or authority when appropriate
Distinction between formal and informal logic
examples: Character Assessment: When character is genuinely relevant (e.g., trustworthiness of a witness)
Expert Testimony: When proper authority is consulted appropriately
Emotional Appeals: When emotion is a legitimate component (e.g., ethical arguments)
Reasonable Consequences: When slippery slope is based on evidence
Practical Dichotomy: When choices are genuinely limited in context
